system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2187-08-14 12:45:00 to 2187-08-16 13:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with inoperable cholangiocarcinoma and a history of recurrent biliary infections, was admitted for progressive fatigue and weakness. Initial workup showed no active infection, with negative blood and urine cultures and only mixed flora in bile. Imaging revealed stable disease but a new L3 vertebral lesion concerning for metastasis, prompting a CT-guided biopsy. He was treated empirically with meropenem for suspected cholangitis, but symptoms did not improve, leading to discontinuation. Iron studies confirmed iron deficiency, and he received two doses of IV ferric gluconate. His pancytopenia worsened, likely due to chronic Bactrim and underlying disease. The portal vein thrombus resolved, but apixaban was continued per oncology. Anxiety and insomnia were managed with Ativan, which he continued at discharge. He was discharged home with services, pending biopsy results, on his baseline regimen including Bactrim, with follow-up for oncology and CBC monitoring.
problems: Migraine, unspecified, not intractable, without status migrainosus

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I've been reviewing why you came in. You had a biliary tube exchange yesterday and developed a fever at home—101.3, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I got chills after I got home. My wife took my temperature and it was high. I took Tylenol and felt better, but she called the oncologist and we came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good call. Given your history of cholangiocarcinoma and past infections, we take fevers seriously. You were given antibiotics in the ER—ertapenem and tigecycline—and now we’re continuing IV meropenem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Bactrim at home to prevent infections. Is this another one of those episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The fever may be from a brief bacterial exposure during the tube exchange. Your labs show your white count dropped a bit—from 6.2 to 3.4—but it’s stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that low? I’ve had low counts before from chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s on the lower side, but not critically so. We’re watching it. Your platelets are also a little low at 64, but not dropping further. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also been having trouble with bowel movements—hard, tarry stools. I’m straining a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I saw that. You had a TURP recently, right? The tarry color is concerning, but your hemoglobin is stable—11.2 on admission, now 12.3—so we don’t think it’s active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But it’s uncomfortable. I feel bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on senna and Miralax to help with the constipation. We’ll also give Gas-X for bloating. Your pantoprazole is continued too, just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. And my pain is just around the tube site—mild, really. I’ve been using the oxycodone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected after the procedure. We’ll keep it on board for now. Your ultrasound this morning showed mild bile duct dilation—same as before—and splenomegaly, which we’ve seen in past scans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No new abscesses or blockages?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing new. The tube looks in place, and the stent is patent as far as we can tell. Your liver enzymes are stable—alkaline phosphatase is up a bit at 236, but not alarming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood cultures? Will those tell us if there’s an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we drew them in the ER. They’ve been negative so far, and you’ve stayed afebrile since. That supports the idea that this was a brief bacteremia, not a full infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might not need the IV antibiotics long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll likely transition you back to your home Bactrim once we’re confident the fever won’t return. That’s our plan if cultures stay negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. You made it through the night without fever—temp stayed around 98.2. Your repeat labs this morning show your white count is holding at 3.5, and platelets improved to 87.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? I feel fine—just a little tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. Your kidney and liver function are stable. Blood cultures are still no growth after 24 hours—very encouraging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So this was probably just a blip from the tube change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what it looks like. We’re going to stop the IV meropenem today and restart your oral Bactrim—same dose you were on at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about the apixaban? I was on that for the blood clot in my portal vein, but stopped it because of low platelets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your platelets are improving, so we’ll discuss with oncology whether to restart it. For now, we’re holding it, but you should follow up with them soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And my urine had some blood and bacteria—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your recent TURP, that’s likely residual inflammation. You’re not having urgency or pain, so we don’t think it’s a UTI. We’ll keep your finasteride and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my headache behind the eye—it’s still there, but mild.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not worsening, and no vision changes—so likely just a tension-type headache. Keep using acetaminophen as needed. If it changes, let us know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, your blood cultures are now negative at 48 hours. That’s excellent. We’re confident this wasn’t a true infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning discharge tomorrow morning. We’ll send you home on your regular meds—Bactrim, ursodiol, dronabinol, and the others.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the constipation meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding Gas-X for bloating and continuing senna and Miralax for now. Use them as needed. If stools stay hard, talk to your PCP about long-term options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up? With oncology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please see Dr. Lee in two weeks. Also, check in with your primary doctor about the apixaban decision and your blood counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. All set for discharge. Your vitals are stable, you’re afebrile, and labs are consistent with improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Just want to make sure I understand—no more IV antibiotics, back to my regular pills, and watch for fever or bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Take all your meds, especially Bactrim. If you develop fever, severe abdominal pain, or black stools, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my wife has your number if she’s worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your discharge instructions list all the warning signs. You’re doing well, Mr. Johnson. Take care at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Get some rest and stay hydrated. We’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with inoperable cholangiocarcinoma and a history of recurrent biliary infections, was admitted for fever (101.3°F) following a routine percutaneous biliary drain (PTBD) exchange. He was afebrile upon arrival and remained so throughout hospitalization. Initial labs showed mild pancytopenia, which stabilized, and liver enzymes were within baseline. Blood cultures remained negative, and ultrasound showed no new biliary obstruction or abscess. The fever was attributed to transient bacteremia post-procedure. Constipation with tarry stools was noted, but no acute gastrointestinal bleed was evident. He was managed with a short course of IV meropenem, then transitioned back to home suppressive Bactrim. Apixaban was held due to prior thrombocytopenia, with recommendation to discuss restart with oncology. He was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up planned.
